rows.R: PP survival at 28 d CI printed -10 to 9.7 pp. From 54/995 vs 51/943 the Wald 95% CI is -2.00 to 2.04 pp (Newcombe -2.03 to 2.05), and P = .985 matches the printed P = .99, so only the CI is wrong. The same Wald method reproduces the ITT CIs and PP ROSC CI exactly. Printed interval is about 5 times too wide and misstates precision.
rows.evidence: jama_jabre_2018_oi_180004.pdf p.6 Table 2 PP survival row (image inspected); p.3 statistical methods; SAP joi180004supp1_prod.pdf p.124.
rows.rationale: Computed in Python: p1 = 5.427%, p2 = 5.408%, SE = 1.029 pp, Wald CI -1.997 to 2.035; Newcombe hybrid score -2.034 to 2.052; two-sided z-test P = 0.985 (printed .99). The same Wald calculation reproduces ITT survival (-1.83 to 2.07; printed -1.8 to 2.1), ITT admission (-7.70 to 0.30), ITT ROSC (-8.83 to -0.49) and PP ROSC (-9.91 to -1.31). Printed -10 to 9.7 cannot arise from these counts by any standard method. Confirmed; substantive because an extracted CI would grossly misstate precision for a PP secondary outcome. Incidental observation outside this candidate: PP survival-to-admission CI computes as -8.16 to 0.08 versus printed -7.6 to 0.6 (P .055 matches), another apparent CI error not adjudicated here.

rows.evidence: jama_jabre_2018_oi_180004.pdf p.6 Table 2 PP ROSC row (image inspected).

rows.R: ETT+stylet denominators: 282/366 for first-attempt success without hypoxemia (Table 3) vs 50/364 for hypoxemia (Table 5). Protocol p.21 excludes patients with missing data only from the relevant outcome; a patient who failed the first attempt is a composite failure even without a valid oximetry waveform. A 2-patient difference is consistent with outcome-specific denominators. Not an error.

The composite requires first-attempt success AND no hypoxemia, so a first-attempt failure (ETT arm had 376-328 = 48 failures) is classifiable as composite failure without oximetry data, while hypoxemia alone is not; 2 such patients would produce 366 vs 364. The bougie arm has 381-373 = 8 failures, so equal denominators there are also plausible. The difference has a satisfactory explanation consistent with the stated plan; exclude (AI suggested retain).

rows.R: Protocol: hypoxemia observed from start of first attempt until 1 minute after ETT cuff inflation (p.9-10). Report (Tables 3, 5; eTable 1): during or within 1 minute after completion of the attempt, with attempt end defined as blade removal. The window end shifts by the short interval between blade removal and cuff inflation; unlikely to change classification. Small definitional difference.
rows.evidence: joi180054supp1_prod.pdf p.9 secondary outcome 1, p.10 measurement procedure; jama_driver_2018_oi_180054.pdf p.7 Table 3 note b, p.9 Table 5 note b; joi180054supp2_prod.pdf p.3 eTable 1 note, p.10 data form (attempt begins/ends with blade).

Threshold and start agree. For successful attempts cuff inflation follows blade removal within seconds, and for failed attempts the protocol endpoint is undefined, so the report's version is a pragmatic restatement. Real but small plan-report difference that I do not consider meaningful for interpretation; L = minor_presentation.

rows.R: Protocol secondary outcome 2: time to intubation from start of attempt to ETT cuff inflation with tube in trachea (successful attempts only by construction). Report: first-attempt duration from blade insertion to blade removal, for all patients including failed attempts, analyzed by Hodges-Lehmann and Cox models. The measured quantity and population differ from the plan.
rows.evidence: joi180054supp1_prod.pdf p.9-10 secondary outcome 2; jama_driver_2018_oi_180054.pdf p.3 Outcomes, p.4 analysis, p.7 Table 3 note c; joi180054supp2_prod.pdf p.3 eTable 1 note, p.10 data form.

The new endpoint excludes post-removal steps to cuff inflation and assigns durations to failed attempts; the article also reports a successful-attempt-only analysis (38 vs 34 s) (median difference 4 s, 95% CI 2 to 7), which is closer to the planned measure but still uses blade removal as the end point. Because the outcome definition changes the quantity compared between arms, I describe this as a substantive difference. Agree with AI.

rows.R: Table 2 SF-36 mental component: effect 6.78 (95% CI 1.64 to 11.92), P = .001. Under the stated dependent t test (N = 27, df 26) the CI implies SE 2.50, t = 2.71, P = .012; even a normal-based CI gives P = .010. Any smaller row n makes P larger. The estimate is the CI midpoint, so the P value is the likely error (.012 vs .001). Inference at CI level unchanged.

P = .001 is incompatible with this CI under any df <= 26 or a z approximation. Confirmed. I rate it minor because the estimate and CI are internally coherent and the significance status at .05 is unchanged; the P value overstates the evidence by about tenfold, so extraction of P would be affected.

rows.R: Table 2 ICU mortality: 132/450 vs 115/458; printed RR 1.11 (0.96-1.27), P = 0.15. Crude RR = 1.17 (Wald 0.94-1.45); chi-square P = 0.15 matches the printed P. Across all 10 RR rows the printed RRs differ from the crude ratios and the CIs are about half the valid width, though note c and Methods describe no adjustment. RR and CI not reproducible.
rows.evidence: jama_simonis_2018_oi_180108.pdf p.6 Table 2 and note c; p.4 Statistical Analysis (images/text inspected).
rows.rationale: Python: crude RR = (132/450)/(115/458) = 1.168; log-scale SE = 0.109, 95% CI 0.94-1.45; uncorrected chi-square P = 0.153 (printed 0.15). Printed CI implies log SE 0.071, roughly half of what these counts allow, so no valid estimator on these data could produce it. Because the printed P values reproduce exactly from the same counts, the counts are not the problem; the RR column (estimate and CI) is wrong or computed by an undisclosed and invalid method. Confirmed. I rate it substantive because the extractable effect estimates and especially their precision are misstated for every binary secondary outcome, even though no conclusion of significance changes.
